source_text: 1. Ostenso manifeste, quod in principio Verbum exsistens apud Deum, per quem omnia facta sunt, qui et semper aderat generi humano, hune in novissimis temporibus secundum prefinitum tempus a Patre, unitum suo plasmati, passibilem hominem factum, exclusa est omnis contradictio dicentium: Si ergo tune natus est, non erat ergo ante Christus. Ostendimus enim, quia non tune ccepit Filius Dei, exsistens semper apud Patrem; sed quando incarnatus est, et homo factus, longam hominum expositionem in seipso recapitulavit, in compendio nobis salutem prestans, ut quod perdideramus in Adam, id est, secundum imaginem et similitudinem esse Dei, hoc in Christo Jesu reciperemus. 2. Quia enim non erat possibile, eum hominem qui semel victus fuerat et elisus per inobedientiam, replasmare, et obtinere Sbravium victoria, iterum autem impossibile erat ut salutem perciperet qui sub peccato ceciderat, utraque operatus est Filius, Verbum Dei exsistens, a Patre descendens, et incarnatus, et usque ad mortem descendens, et dispensationem consummans salutis nostre, cui credere nos indubitate adhortans, iterum ®dicit: Ne dixeris in corde tuo, Quis ascendit in celum? hoc est Christum deducere. Aut, Quis descendit in abyssum? hoe est Christum a mortuis liberare; deinde infert: Quoniam si confitearis in ore tuo Dominum Jesum, et credideris in corde tuo, quoniam Deus illum excitavit a mortuis, salvous eris. Et rationem reddidit propter quam causam hee fecit Verbum Dei, dicens: Jn hoc enim * Christus et vixit, et mortwus est, et resurrexit, ut vivorum et mortuorum dominetur. Et iterum ad Corinthios scribens ait : Vos autem annuntiamus Christum * Jesum crucifizum. Et infert: Oalix benedictionis quem benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis est Christi? Quis est autem qui communicavit nobis de escis? Utrum is qui ab illis affingitur sursum Christus, superextensus Horo, id est fini, et formavit eorum matrem: an VETO qui ex virgine est Emmanuel, qui butyrum et mel manduCavit, de quo ait propheta: Et homo est, et quis cognoscet eum? Hic idem a Paulo annuntiabatur: Zradidi enim, inquit, vobis in primis, quoniam Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris secundum Scripturas, et quoniam sepultus est, et resurrewit tertia die secwndum Scripturas. 3. Manifestum est igitur, quoniam Paulus alterum Christum nescit, nisi hune solum, qui et passus est, et sepultus est, et resurrexit, qui et natus est, quem et hominem dixit. Cum enim dixisset: Si autem Christus annuntiatur quoniam a mortuis resurrexit, intulit, rationem reddens incarnationis ejus: Quoniam per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Et ubique in passione Domini nostri, et humanitate, et mortificatione ejus, Christi usus est nomine, quemadmodum in illo: Noli esca tua perdere illum, pro quo Christus mortuus est. Et iterum: Nune autem in Christo vos qui aliquando fuistis longe, facti estis proximi in sanguine Christi. Et iterum: Christus nos redemit de maledicto Legis, factus pro nobis maledictum: quoniam scriptum est, Maledictus omnis qui pendet in ligno. Et iterum: Et periet infirmus in tua scientia frater, propter quem Ohristus mortuus est; significans, quoniam non Christus impassibilis descendit in Jesum, sed ipse, Jesus Christus cum esset, passus est pro nobis, qui decubuit et resurrexit, qui descendit et ascendit, Filius Dei, filius hominis factus: quemadmodum et ipsum nomen significat. In Christi enim nomine subauditur qui unxit, et ipse qui unctus est, et ipsa unctio in qua unctus est. Et unxit quidem Pater, unctus est vero Filius, in Spiritu, qui est unctio; quemadmodum per Esaiam ait sermo: Spiritus Dei super me, propter quod unwit me; significans et unguentem Patrem, et unctum Filium, et unctionem, qui est Spiritus. 4. Et ipse autem Dominus manifestum facit eum qui est passus. Cum enim interrogasset discipulos: Quem me homines dicunt esse Filium Hominis? ®et Petrus cum respondisset: Ju es Christus Filius Dei vivi; et cum laudatus esset ab eo, Quoniam caro et sanguis non revelavit ei, sed Pater qui est in coelis, manifestum fecit, quoniam Filius Hominis hie est Christus Filius Dei vivi: He eo enim, inquit, capit demonstrare discentibus, quoniam oportet illum Hierosolymam ire, et multa pati a sacerdotibus, 1 et reprobari, et crucifigi, et tertia die resurgere. Ipse qui agnitus est a Petro Christus, qui eum beatum dixit, quoniam Pater ei revelavit Filium Dei vivi, dixit, semetipsum oportere multa pati et crucifigi: et tune Petro increpavit, secundum opinionem hominum putanti eum esse Christum, et passionem ejus ayersanti, et dixit discipulis: Si gwis eult post me venire, neget se, et tollat crucom suam, et sequatur me. Qui enim voluerit animam suam salvare, perdet illam: et qui eam perdiderit propter me, salvabit eam. Hee enim Christus manifeste dicebat, ipse exsistens Salvator eorum, qui propter suam confessionem in mortem traderentur, et perderent animas suas.
pass_a_gloss: It is shown manifestly, that in the beginning the Word existing with God, through whom all things were made, who also always was present with the human race, this one in the last times according to the predetermined time from the Father, united with his own creature, made a passible man, every contradiction of those saying is excluded: If therefore he was born then, he was not therefore before Christ. For we show that the Son of God did not begin then, existing always with the Father; but when he was incarnated and made man, he recapitulated in himself the long exposition of men, providing salvation for us in brief, so that what we lost in Adam, that is, to be according to the image and likeness of God, this we might receive in Christ Jesus. For since it was not possible for man, who had once been conquered and defeated through disobedience, to be remade and to obtain the victory of the Savior, and it was again impossible for him who had fallen under sin to perceive salvation, the Son, the Word of God existing, descending from the Father, and incarnated, and descending even to death, and consummating the dispensation of our salvation, to which we are undoubtedly exhorted to believe, says again: Do not say in your heart, Who ascends into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down. Or, Who descends into the abyss? that is, to liberate Christ from the dead; then he adds: For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. And he gives the reason for which cause the Word of God did these things, saying: For in this Christ both lived and died and rose again, so that he might be the Lord of the living and the dead. And again, writing to the Corinthians, he says: But we proclaim Christ Jesus crucified. And he adds: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion of the blood of Christ? Who is it that has communion with us from the foods? Is it he who is affixed from those above, Christ, extended over the horizon, that is, the end, and formed their mother: or is it he who is from the virgin, Emmanuel, who ate butter and honey, about whom the prophet says: And he is a man, and who will know him? This same one was announced by Paul: For I delivered to you in the first place, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures. It is therefore manifest that Paul knows no other Christ, except this one alone, who both suffered and was buried and rose again, who also was born, whom he also called a man. For when he had said: If Christ is proclaimed as having risen from the dead, he introduced, giving the reason for his incarnation: For through man death, and through man the resurrection of the dead. And everywhere in the passion of our Lord and his humanity and his mortification, the name of Christ is used, just as in that: Do not lose your food for him for whom Christ died. And again: But now in Christ you who once were far off have been made near in the blood of Christ. And again: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. And again: And the weak brother will perish in your knowledge, for whom Christ died; signifying that it was not the impassible Christ who descended into Jesus, but he himself, Jesus Christ, who was passible, suffered for us, who lay down and rose again, who descended and ascended, the Son of God, made the son of man: just as the name itself also signifies. For in the name of Christ is implied he who anointed, and he who was anointed, and the anointing in which he was anointed. And the Father anointed, the Son was anointed, in the Spirit, who is the anointing; just as the word says through Isaiah: The Spirit of God is upon me, because he anointed me; signifying both the anointing Father and the anointed Son and the anointing, which is the Spirit. And the Lord himself makes manifest the one who suffered. For when he asked the disciples: Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am? and Peter responded: You are Christ, the Son of the living God; and when he was praised by him, Because flesh and blood did not reveal it to him, but the Father who is in heaven, he made manifest that the Son of Man here is Christ, the Son of the living God: For he says, beginning to show the disciples that it is necessary for him to go to Jerusalem and to suffer many things from the priests, and to be rejected, and to be crucified, and to rise again on the third day. He himself, who was recognized by Peter as Christ, who said he was blessed, because the Father revealed to him the Son of the living God, said that it was necessary for him to suffer many things and to be crucified: and then he rebuked Peter, thinking according to human opinion that he was Christ, and denying his passion, and said to the disciples: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wants to save his soul will lose it: and whoever loses it for my sake will save it. For Christ was saying these things manifestly, he himself being the Savior of those who would be handed over to death for his sake, and would lose their souls.

pass_b_english: It is plainly demonstrated that the Word existed with God in the beginning and made all things, and that he was always present with the human race. In the last times, at the Father's appointed hour, this Word united himself with his own creature and became a passible man. That fact excludes every objection from those who ask: 'If he was born then, he did not exist before as Christ.' We prove that the Son of God did not begin to exist at that moment, since he existed always with the Father. When he became incarnate and was made man, he recapitulated the long history of humanity in himself, providing our salvation in a concise way, so that what we lost in Adam — namely, being according to the image and likeness of God — we might recover in Christ Jesus. (John 1:1–3; Romans 5:14–19)

Since it was impossible for man, once conquered and defeated through disobedience, to be remade and to obtain the victory of the Savior, and equally impossible for one who had fallen under sin to attain salvation, the Son — the Word of God — undertook both tasks. Existing eternally, he descended from the Father, became incarnate, descended even to death, and brought the dispensation of our salvation to completion. He exhorts us without doubt to believe in this, and says again: 'Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?" (that is, to bring Christ down) or "Who will descend into the abyss?" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).' He then adds: 'If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.' (Deuteronomy 30:12–14; Romans 10:6–9)

He also gives the reason why the Word of God did these things: 'For this purpose Christ both lived and died and rose again, so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead.' Writing again to the Corinthians he says: 'We proclaim Christ crucified.' He adds: 'The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ?' Who shares with us in these things? Is it the one who is fabricated from above, a Christ stretched across the horizon — that is, the end — who formed their mother? Or is it the one from the virgin, Emmanuel, who ate butter and honey, of whom the prophet says: 'He is a man, and who can know him?' (Isaiah 7:14–15). This same one was announced by Paul: 'For I delivered to you as of first importance that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.' (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)

It is therefore clear that Paul knows no other Christ except this one alone — the one who suffered, was buried, and rose again, who was also born and whom he calls a man. When he had said, 'If Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead,' he supplied the reason for his incarnation: 'For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man.' Everywhere, in the passion of our Lord, in his humanity, and in his mortification, he uses the name Christ — as in: 'Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died,' and again: 'Now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ,' and again: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."' (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). And again: 'The weak brother perishes through your knowledge, the one for whom Christ died' — signifying that it was not an impassible Christ who descended into Jesus, but Jesus Christ himself, who was passible, suffered for us, lay down and rose again, descended and ascended, the Son of God made the Son of Man, just as the name itself signifies. For in the name Christ is implied the one who anoints (the Father), the one anointed (the Son), and the anointing (the Spirit). The Father anointed, the Son was anointed, in the Spirit who is the anointing, just as the word says through Isaiah: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me' — signifying both the anointing Father, the anointed Son, and the anointing, which is the Spirit. (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18)

The Lord himself makes manifest the one who suffered. When he asked his disciples, 'Who do people say that the Son of Man is?' and Peter answered, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,' Jesus praised him: 'Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in heaven.' He thus made clear that the Son of Man is the Christ, the Son of the living God. From that point he began to show the disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the priests, be rejected, be crucified, and rise on the third day. The very one whom Peter recognized as Christ — whom he called blessed because the Father had revealed the Son of the living God to him — declared that he himself must suffer and be crucified. Then he rebuked Peter, who was thinking by human opinion that Jesus was the Christ while denying his passion, and said to the disciples: 'If anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.' Christ said these things plainly, himself being the Savior of those who would be handed over to death for his confession and would lose their lives. (Matthew 16:13–25)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the nuances of the Christological arguments regarding the passibility of the Word and the distinction between the eternal Word and the incarnate Son. All scripture citations in Pass B correspond to the quoted or alluded text in the Latin (e.g., Romans 10:9 for 'confitearis in ore tuo Dominum Jesum', Isaiah 7:14 for 'de quo ait propheta: Et homo est...', etc.). The title 'The Incarnation of the Word' correctly identifies the central thought of the passage.
